patterns.label: I want to…
patterns.note: The most useful starter — attach any verb to express what you want to do.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 soeng2 ▢.
drills.english: I want to watch a movie.

patterns.label: I'll have / I need…
patterns.note: Use for ordering food, asking for things, or stating what you need.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 jiu3 ▢
drills.english: I'll have water

patterns.label: Do you have…?
patterns.note: A very natural way to ask about availability — literally 'have or not have?'

drills.frameJ: jau5 mou5 ▢?
drills.english: Do you have dim sum?

patterns.label: Where is…?
patterns.note: Put the thing you're looking for at the start, then ask where it is.

examples.j: sai2 sau2 gaan1 hai2 bin1 dou6?
dei6 tit3 zaam6 hai2 bin1 dou6?

drills.frameJ: ▢ hai2 bin1 dou6?
drills.english: Where is the MTR?

patterns.label: How much?
patterns.note: Works alone or after pointing at something. Add ni1 go3 (this one) for clarity.

patterns.label: Please give me…
patterns.note: Very common in restaurants and shops. Note how 'me' comes at the end.

examples.j: m4 goi1 bei2 bui1 caa4 ngo5
examples.e: Please give me a cup of tea

examples.j: m4 goi1 bei2 go3 doi2 ngo5
m4 goi1 bei2 faai3 zi2 ngo5

patterns.label: Very…
patterns.note: hou2 intensifies any adjective. Stack it for extra emphasis — hou2 hou2 means 'very very good'.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: I'm very tired.

drills.frameJ: gam1 jat6 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: It's very hot today.

patterns.label: Not / Don't…
patterns.note: m4 is the general negation particle. Place it directly before the verb or adjective.

patterns.label: Yes/no question
patterns.note: Add maa3 to the end of any statement to turn it into a yes/no question.

examples.j: nei5 sik1 gong2 gwong2 dung1 waa6 maa3?

patterns.label: What would you like to…?
patterns.note: A polite way to ask what someone wants — common in service situations.

examples.e: What would you like to eat?
What would you like to drink?
What would you like to buy?

patterns.label: I feel…
patterns.note: Use this to describe how you're feeling physically or emotionally.

examples.j: ngo5 gok3 dak1 m4 syu1 fuk6

drills.frameJ: ngo5 gok3 dak1 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: I feel really happy.

patterns.label: Going to…
patterns.note: Simple and direct. Works for saying where you're going or asking where to go.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 heoi3 ▢.
drills.english: I'm going to the hotel.

patterns.label: See you at / on…
patterns.note: Put any time word before gin3 to arrange when to meet.

patterns.label: Is that ok / Can I?
patterns.note: Literally 'ok or not ok?' — use to seek permission or check if something works.

examples.j: ngo5 co5 hai2 ni1 dou6 dak1 m4 dak1?
ji4 gaa1 heoi3 dak1 m4 dak1?

patterns.label: Too…!
patterns.note: Express that something is excessive. laa3 adds a sense of finality or mild complaint.

drills.frameJ: taai3 ▢ laa3!
drills.english: Too expensive!

patterns.label: Can I / May I…?
patterns.note: A polite way to ask permission — more formal than dak1 m4 dak1.

examples.j: ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 gong2 maan6 di1?
ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 tai2 haa5?
ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 dang2 ngo5?

patterns.label: What is…?
patterns.note: Use when you want to know what something is called or what something means.

examples.j: ni1 go3 zi6 hai6 mat1 je5?

patterns.label: Why…?
patterns.note: Place dim2 gaai3 at the start of any statement to turn it into a 'why' question.

patterns.label: There's also… / And also…
patterns.note: Use to add something on top of what's already been said — great for ordering.

drills.frameJ: zung6 jau5 ▢.
drills.english: There's also noodles.

patterns.label: A bit more / less…
patterns.note: Adding di1 after an adjective softens it — useful for polite requests.

patterns.label: I like…
patterns.note: Express preferences for things, food, activities or people.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 zung1 ji3 ▢.
drills.english: I like dogs.

patterns.label: Give [someone] [something]
patterns.note: bei2 means 'give' or 'let'. The person receiving comes at the end — opposite to English.

patterns.label: I will…
patterns.note: Use wui5 to talk about future intentions or promises.

patterns.label: Have never / Not yet done
patterns.note: mei6...gwo expresses something you haven't experienced yet. Very useful for travel.

patterns.label: Already done…
patterns.note: zo2 marks completion — something has already happened. laa3 adds a sense of 'just now'.

patterns.label: How long?
patterns.note: Use to ask about duration — how long something takes or lasts.

examples.e: How long do I have to wait?
How long does it take to get there?

patterns.label: Together / Let's…
patterns.note: jat1 cai4 means 'together' — add it before any verb to suggest doing something jointly.

examples.e: Come on, let's do it together

patterns.label: First… then…
patterns.note: sin1 means 'first' and zoi3 means 'then/again' — use them to sequence actions.

patterns.label: I think…
patterns.note: ngo5 lam2 softly expresses an opinion or guess — less certain than stating a fact.

patterns.label: Wait a moment / Wait for…
patterns.note: dang2 means 'wait'. Use alone for 'wait a moment' or add who/how long to wait.

patterns.label: Greet, then speak
patterns.note: Cantonese conversations open with a greeting before getting to the point. Lead with a greeting, then say what you came to say.

examples.j: zou2 san4! sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6?
examples.e: Good morning! Have you eaten yet?

examples.j: nei5 hou2! hou2 noi6 mou5 gin3.

drills.frameJ: ▢! ngo5 giu3 William.
drills.english: Hello! My name is William.

patterns.label: Match the time of day
patterns.note: Cantonese greetings change with the time of day — 早晨 (zou2 san4) in the morning, 晚上好 (maan5 soeng6 hou2) in the evening. Pick the one that fits.

examples.j: zou2 san4! fan3 dak1 hou2 maa3?
examples.e: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

examples.j: maan5 soeng6 hou2! sik6 zo2 faan6 mei6?
zou2 san4! gam1 jat6 faan1 gung1 aa3?

drills.frameJ: ▢! fan3 dak1 hou2 maa3?
drills.english: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

patterns.label: Apologise
patterns.note: 對唔住 (deoi3 m4 zyu6) means 'sorry'. Lead with it, then explain — just like in English.

examples.j: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 ci4 dou3.
deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 m4 zi1.
deoi3 m4 zyu6, m4 goi1 ze3 gwo3.
examples.e: Sorry — excuse me, let me through.

drills.frameJ: ▢, ngo5 ci4 dou3.
drills.english: Sorry, I'm late.

patterns.label: Respond to thanks
patterns.note: When someone says 多謝 (do1 ze6), the natural reply is 唔緊要 (m4 gan2 jiu3) — 'it's nothing / you're welcome'.

examples.j: m4 gan2 jiu3, siu2 si6 laa1.
m4 gan2 jiu3, m4 sai2 haak3 hei3.
examples.e: You're welcome, no need to be formal.

drills.frameJ: do1 ze6! — ▢.
drills.english: Thank you! — You're welcome.

patterns.label: Close a conversation
patterns.note: 再見 (zoi3 gin3) ends a conversation. It often follows a thank-you — 多謝，再見 (do1 ze6, zoi3 gin3)!

drills.frameJ: do1 ze6, ▢!
drills.english: Thank you, goodbye!

patterns.label: Answer yes or no
patterns.note: Cantonese has no single word for 'yes'. Reply with 係 (hai6, 'it is') or 唔係 (m4 hai6, 'it isn't') to a 係 (hai6) question.

drills.frameJ: keoi5 hai6 m4 hai6 hok6 saang1? — ▢.
drills.english: Is he a student? — Yes.

patterns.label: Say if it's OK
patterns.note: 得 (dak1) means 'OK / can do', 唔得 (m4 dak1) means 'no / can't'. A single word answers a 得唔得 (dak1 m4 dak1) question.

drills.frameJ: ji4 gaa1 heoi3 dak1 m4 dak1? — ▢.
drills.english: Can we go now? — Sure.

patterns.label: Get attention politely
patterns.note: 唔該 (m4 goi1) is the everyday 'excuse me / please' — use it to get attention or ask for service. (多謝 (do1 ze6) is for thanking someone for a gift.)

drills.frameJ: ▢, ze3 gwo3.
drills.english: Excuse me, let me through.

patterns.label: Welcome someone
patterns.note: 歡迎 (fun1 jing4) means 'welcome'. Shops greet customers with the set phrase 歡迎光臨 (fun1 jing4 gwong1 lam4) — 'welcome to our shop'.

drills.frameJ: ▢ gwong1 lam4!
drills.english: Welcome (to our shop)!

patterns.label: Invite politely
patterns.note: 請 (cing2) is the formal 'please', placed before a verb — 請坐 (cing2 co5, please sit), 請講 (cing2 gong2, please speak). More formal than 唔該 (m4 goi1).

drills.frameJ: ▢ co5.
drills.english: Please sit down.

patterns.label: Counting up
patterns.note: Cantonese counts the same way you'd recite numbers in English: 一二三四五 (jat1 ji6 saam1 sei3 ng5). The first ten numbers are the foundation for every larger number.

drills.frameJ: jat1, ji6, ▢, sei3, ng5.
drills.english: One, two, three, four, five.

patterns.label: How many? (幾多 gei2 do1)
patterns.note: 幾多 (gei2 do1) is the all-purpose 'how many / how much' question word. Use it before a classifier or noun to ask about quantity.

examples.j: nei5 jau5 gei2 do1 bun2 syu1?
examples.e: How many books do you have?

drills.frameJ: nei5 jau5 ▢ bun2 syu1?
drills.english: How many books do you have?

patterns.label: Saying a dollar amount
patterns.note: 蚊 (man1) is the colloquial word for Hong Kong dollars. Just put a number in front: 十蚊 (sap6 man1, ten dollars), 一百蚊 (jat1 baak3 man1, a hundred dollars).

drills.frameJ: ni1 go3 ▢ man1.
drills.english: This is one hundred dollars.

patterns.label: Half (一半 jat1 bun3)
patterns.note: 一半 (jat1 bun3) means 'half'. Use it before a measure word + noun to say half of something — 一半個西瓜 (jat1 bun3 go3 sai1 gwaa1) = half a watermelon.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sik6 zo2 ▢ go3 sai1 gwaa1.
drills.english: I ate half of the watermelon.

patterns.label: Multiples of ten
patterns.note: For 20, 30, 50 — just put the digit in front of 十 (sap6): 二十 (ji6 sap6, twenty), 三十 (saam1 sap6, thirty), 五十 (ng5 sap6, fifty). Same pattern as English 'twen-ty', 'thir-ty'.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 jau5 ▢ man1.
drills.english: I have fifty dollars.

patterns.label: Asking someone's name
patterns.note: The standard opener for meeting someone new — 'What's your name?' literally 'you called what name?'

examples.j: cing2 man6 nei5 giu3 mat1 meng2?

drills.frameJ: A: ▢ B: ngo5 giu3 William.
drills.english: What is your name? — My name is William.

patterns.label: Introducing yourself
patterns.note: 我叫 (ngo5 giu3) … is the natural way to introduce yourself — literally 'I'm called…'. Just add your name.

examples.j: nei5 hou2, ngo5 giu3 siu2 ming4.

drills.frameJ: A: nei5 giu3 mat1 meng2? B: ▢ William.
drills.english: What's your name? — My name is William.

patterns.label: How are you?
patterns.note: The standard 'How are you?' greeting after the initial 你好 (nei5 hou2). Add 嗎 (maa3) to turn 'you good' into a yes/no question.

examples.j: nei5 hou2 maa3? — ngo5 hou2 hou2.

drills.frameJ: A: ▢ B: ngo5 hou2 hou2, do1 ze6!
drills.english: How are you? — I'm well, thanks!

patterns.label: When you don't understand
patterns.note: 我唔明 (ngo5 m4 ming4) is a polite, useful phrase to flag that you didn't catch what was said. Often paired with 請講慢啲 (cing2 gong2 maan6 di1) — 'please speak slowly'.

examples.j: deoi3 m4 zyu6, ngo5 m4 ming4.
ngo5 m4 ming4, cing2 gong2 maan6 di1.
examples.e: I don't understand, please speak slowly.

drills.frameJ: ▢, cing2 gong2 maan6 di1.
drills.english: I don't understand — please speak slowly.

patterns.label: Asking the price
patterns.note: 幾錢 (gei2 cin2)？ literally 'how much money?' — the universal way to ask the price of anything at a shop or restaurant.

drills.frameJ: A: ▢ B: ng5 sap6 man1.
drills.english: How much? — Fifty dollars.

patterns.label: Who? (邊個 bin1 go3)
patterns.note: 邊個 (bin1 go3) means 'who / which one'. Place it where the unknown person goes in the sentence.

examples.j: bin1 go3 hai6 nei5 ge3 lou5 si1?

drills.frameJ: ▢ hai6 nei5 ge3 lou5 si1?
drills.english: Who is your teacher?

patterns.label: What? (乜嘢 mat1 je5)
patterns.note: 乜嘢 (mat1 je5) means 'what'. In Cantonese it usually goes at the END of the question — not the beginning like English. 你食乜嘢 (nei5 sik6 mat1 je5)? = 'You eat what?'

drills.frameJ: ni1 go3 hai6 ▢?
drills.english: What is this?

patterns.label: Where? (邊度 bin1 dou6)
patterns.note: 邊度 (bin1 dou6) means 'where'. Like 乜嘢 (mat1 je5), it usually goes at the end of the question in Cantonese.

drills.frameJ: nei5 zyu6 hai2 ▢?
drills.english: Where do you live?

patterns.label: When? (幾時 gei2 si4)
patterns.note: 幾時 (gei2 si4) means 'when'. Often appears at the start: 幾時去食飯 (gei2 si4 heoi3 sik6 faan6)? = 'When are we going to eat?'

examples.e: When are we going to eat?

drills.frameJ: ▢ heoi3 sik6 faan6?
drills.english: When are we going to eat?

patterns.label: Why? (點解 dim2 gaai2)
patterns.note: 點解 (dim2 gaai2) means 'why' — literally 'how to explain'. Use it to ask the reason for something.

drills.frameJ: nei5 ▢ m4 lai4?
drills.english: Why aren't you coming?

patterns.label: Introducing a family member
patterns.note: 呢個係我 (ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5) … is the everyday way to introduce someone — literally 'this one is my…'. Add the family word at the end.

examples.j: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 baa4 baa1.
ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 maa4 maa1.
ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 sai3 lou2.

drills.frameJ: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 ▢.
drills.english: This is my father.

patterns.label: Talking about parents
patterns.note: To talk about your mum or dad, just say 我媽媽 (ngo5 maa4 maa1) / 我爸爸 (ngo5 baa4 baa1) — no possessive particle needed. The relationship is built in.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa1 hou2 sek3 ngo5.
examples.e: My mother loves me very much.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa1 zyu2 faan6 hou2 hou2 sik6.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢ hou2 sek3 ngo5.
drills.english: My mother loves me very much.

patterns.label: Talking about siblings
patterns.note: Cantonese distinguishes elder and younger siblings with separate words — 哥哥 (go4 go1, older brother), 弟弟 (dai6 dai2, younger brother), 姐姐 (ze4 ze1, older sister), 妹妹 (mui4 mui2, younger sister). No ambiguity, but you have to know which.

examples.j: ngo5 go4 go1 duk6 daai6 hok6.
examples.e: My older brother is in university.

examples.j: ngo5 mui4 mui2 hou2 ho2 oi3.
examples.e: My younger sister is very cute.

examples.j: ngo5 jau5 jat1 go3 ze4 ze1.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢ bei2 ngo5 daai6 loeng5 seoi3.
drills.english: My older brother is two years older than me.
drills.frameE: My … is two years older than me.

patterns.label: Grandparents (paternal vs maternal)
patterns.structure: je4 je2 / maa4 maa2 / ngoi6 gung1 / ngoi6 po4
patterns.note: Cantonese has different words for paternal and maternal grandparents. 爺爺 (je4 je2) / 嫲嫲 (maa4 maa2) are your father's parents; 外公 (ngoi6 gung1) / 外婆 (ngoi6 po4) — where 外 (ngoi6) means 'outside' — are your mother's. The distinction matters in conversation.

examples.j: ngo5 je4 je2 zyu6 hai2 hoeng1 haa5.
examples.e: My (paternal) grandfather lives in the village.

examples.j: ngo5 maa4 maa2 zyu2 faan6 hou2 hou2 sik6.
ngo5 ngoi6 po4 hou2 sek3 ngo5.
examples.e: My (maternal) grandmother loves me very much.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢ zyu6 hai2 hoeng1 haa5.
drills.english: My paternal grandfather lives in the village.

patterns.label: Talking about your children
patterns.note: To say how many children you have, use 我有 (ngo5 jau5) + [number] + 個 (go3) + 兒子 (ji4 zi2, son) / 女兒 (neoi5 ji4, daughter). 個 (go3) is the all-purpose classifier for people.

examples.j: ngo5 jau5 jat1 go3 ji4 zi2.
ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 neoi5 ji4.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 jau5 loeng5 go3 ▢.
drills.english: I have two daughters.

patterns.label: Today / tomorrow / yesterday
patterns.structure: gam1 jat6 / ting1 jat6 / kam4 jat6 + …
patterns.note: The three everyday time anchors: 今日 (gam1 jat6, today), 聽日 (ting1 jat6, tomorrow), 琴日 (kam4 jat6, yesterday). Put one at the start of a sentence to set when.

drills.frameJ: ▢ gin3!
drills.english: See you tomorrow!

patterns.label: Days of the week
patterns.note: Days are built from 星期 (sing1 kei4, week) + a number: 星期一 (sing1 kei4 jat1, Monday) through 星期六 (sing1 kei4 luk6, Saturday). Sunday breaks the pattern — 星期日 (sing1 kei4 jat6).

drills.frameJ: ngo5 dei6 ▢ heoi3 jam2 caa4.
drills.english: We go for dim sum on Sunday.
drills.frameE: We go for dim sum on …

patterns.label: Morning / night
patterns.note: 朝早 (ziu1 zou2) is the morning, 夜晚 (je6 maan5) is the night. Use them to say when in the day something happens.

drills.frameJ: ▢ sik6 zou2 caan1.
drills.english: Eat breakfast in the morning.

patterns.label: This / next time reference
patterns.note: Stack a time word in front of an activity to schedule it: 聽日 (ting1 jat6, tomorrow) + the plan. Cantonese keeps the time word first, like 'tomorrow I go'.

drills.frameJ: ▢ lok6 jyu5.
drills.english: It rained yesterday.

patterns.label: Naming a weekday
patterns.note: To state today's day: 今日星期… (gam1 jat6 sing1 kei4 …). 今日 (gam1 jat6) sets 'today', then the weekday follows.

drills.frameJ: gam1 jat6 ▢, jiu3 faan1 gung1.
drills.english: Today is Monday, have to work.

patterns.label: Completed action (咗 zo2)
patterns.note: 咗 (zo2) after a verb marks it as done — like English '-ed'. 食咗 (sik6 zo2) = ate, 去咗 (heoi3 zo2) = went. The single most useful tense marker.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sik6 ▢ faan6.
drills.english: I have eaten.

patterns.label: In progress (緊 gan2)
patterns.note: 緊 (gan2) after a verb means the action is happening right now — like English '-ing'. 食緊 (sik6 gan2) = eating, 做緊 (zou6 gan2) = doing.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sik6 ▢ faan6, dang2 zan6 sin1.
drills.english: I'm eating right now, wait a bit.

patterns.label: Have you ever… (過 gwo3)
patterns.note: 過 (gwo3) after a verb marks past experience — 'have you ever…'. 食過 (sik6 gwo3) = have eaten (before), 去過 (heoi3 gwo3) = have been to.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 heoi3 ▢ hoeng1 gong2.
drills.english: I've been to Hong Kong before.

patterns.label: Will / going to (會 wui5)
patterns.note: 會 (wui5) before a verb marks the future — 'will / would'. 我會去 (ngo5 wui5 heoi3) = I will go. For obligation use 要 (jiu3, need to) instead.

drills.frameJ: ting1 jat6 ▢ lok6 jyu5.
drills.english: It will rain tomorrow.

patterns.label: Already / not yet (已經 ji5 ging1 / 未 mei6)
patterns.note: 已經 (ji5 ging1, already) and 未 (mei6, not yet) are a natural pair for answering 'done or not?'. 已經食咗 (ji5 ging1 sik6 zo2) = already eaten; 未食 (mei6 sik6) = haven't eaten yet.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢ sik6 zo2 laa3.
drills.english: I've already eaten.

patterns.label: Yes/no question (嗎 maa3)
patterns.note: 嗎 (maa3) at the end of a statement turns it into a yes/no question — the simplest way to ask. 你好 (nei5 hou2, you're well) + 嗎 (maa3) = 你好嗎 (nei5 hou2 maa3, are you well?).

drills.frameJ: nei5 sik6 zo2 faan6 ▢?
drills.english: Have you eaten?

patterns.label: Softening a suggestion (啦 laa1)
patterns.note: 啦 (laa1) softens a suggestion or request into something friendly — 'come on, let's…'. 走啦 (zau2 laa1) = let's go (gently urging).

drills.frameJ: ngo5 dei6 zau2 ▢!
drills.english: Let's get going!

patterns.label: Completion / change (喇 laa3)
patterns.note: 喇 (laa3) signals something has changed or is now the case — 'now' or completion. 好喇 (hou2 laa3) = OK now / that's enough.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sik6 baau2 ▢.
drills.english: I'm full now.

patterns.label: Surprised question (咩 me1)
patterns.note: 咩 (me1) at the end expresses surprise or doubt — 'really? / is that so?'. 真係咩 (zan1 hai6 me1) = is that really true?

drills.frameJ: keoi5 zau2 zo2 ▢? zan1 hai6 gu2 m4 dou2.
drills.english: He's left, really? I'm surprised.

patterns.label: Matter-of-fact (㗎 gaa3)
patterns.note: 㗎 (gaa3) states something as plain fact — 'that's just how it is'. 係㗎 (hai6 gaa3) = yes, that's right (firmly).

drills.frameJ: keoi5 hai6 lou5 si1 ▢, m4 hou2 waai4 ji4.
drills.english: He's a teacher, that's a fact — don't doubt it.
drills.frameE: He's a teacher … — don't doubt it.

patterns.label: Naming a colour
patterns.note: Colour words all end in 色 (sik1, colour): 紅色 (hung4 sik1, red), 藍色 (laam4 sik1, blue). Say 呢個係… (ni1 go3 hai6 …, this is …) to name one.

examples.j: keoi5 gin6 saam1 hai6 laam4 sik1.

drills.frameJ: siu1 fong4 ce1 hai6 ▢.
drills.english: The fire truck is red.

patterns.label: Colour of nature
patterns.note: Useful for describing the world: 天空 (tin1 hung1, sky) is 藍色 (laam4 sik1, blue), grass is 綠色 (luk6 sik1, green).

drills.frameJ: tin1 hung1 hai6 ▢.
drills.english: The sky is blue.

patterns.label: Light and dark colours
patterns.note: 白色 (baak6 sik1, white) and 黑色 (hak1 sik1, black) are the two extremes — handy for clothes and basic description.

drills.frameJ: je6 maan5 tin1 hou2 hak1, hai6 ▢.
drills.english: The night sky is dark — it's black.
drills.frameE: The night sky is dark — it's …

patterns.label: Stating a favourite colour
patterns.note: 我鍾意 (ngo5 zung1 ji3, I like) + a colour states a preference. Swap the colour to talk about what you or others like.

examples.j: keoi5 zung1 ji3 fan2 hung4 sik1.
ngo5 m4 zung1 ji3 caang2 sik1.

drills.english: I like purple, like grapes.

patterns.label: Warm colours
patterns.note: The warm end of the spectrum: 紅色 (hung4 sik1, red), 橙色 (caang2 sik1, orange), 黃色 (wong4 sik1, yellow). Note 橙 (caang2) also means 'orange' the fruit.

examples.j: cau1 tin1 jau5 hou2 do1 caang2 sik1.

drills.frameJ: hoeng1 ziu1 hai6 ▢.
drills.english: A banana is yellow.

patterns.label: Ordering a drink your way
patterns.structure: [drink] + gaa1 bing1 / siu2 bing1 / zau2 tim4
patterns.note: Cha chaan teng customisation: 加冰 (gaa1 bing1, add ice), 少冰 (siu2 bing1, less ice), 走甜 (zau2 tim4, no sugar). Tack one onto your drink order.

drills.frameJ: dung3 gaa3 fe1 ▢, m4 hou2 taai3 tim4.
drills.english: Iced coffee, no sugar — not too sweet.

patterns.label: Hot or cold drink
patterns.note: 熱飲 (jit6 jam2) is a hot drink, 凍飲 (dung3 jam2) is a cold one — the first choice a server asks about. 熱 (jit6) = hot, 凍 (dung3) = cold.

dung3 tin1 jam2 jit6 jam2 hou2.

drills.frameJ: hou2 dung3 aa3, ngo5 jiu3 ▢.
drills.english: It's cold — I'll have a hot drink.

patterns.label: Full or hungry
patterns.note: Two states around eating: 餓 (ngo6, hungry) before, 飽 (baau2, full) after. 我好餓 (ngo5 hou2 ngo6) = I'm very hungry; 我食飽喇 (ngo5 sik6 baau2 laa3) = I'm full now.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 sing4 jat6 mei6 sik6 faan6, hou2 ▢.

patterns.label: Describing someone's character
patterns.note: 佢好 (keoi5 hou2, he/she is very) + a character word describes a person: 善良 (sin6 loeng4, kind), 聰明 (cung1 ming4, smart), 搞笑 (gaau2 siu3, funny).

drills.frameJ: keoi5 sing4 jat6 bong1 jan4, hou2 ▢.
drills.english: She always helps people, she's very kind.
drills.frameE: She always helps people, she's very …

patterns.label: Worried or nervous
patterns.structure: ngo5 hou2 + daam1 sam1 / gan2 zoeng1
patterns.note: Two anxious feelings: 擔心 (daam1 sam1, worried — about something) and 緊張 (gan2 zoeng1, nervous — keyed up). 我好擔心 (ngo5 hou2 daam1 sam1) = I'm very worried.

drills.frameJ: ting1 jat6 haau2 si5, ngo5 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: Exam tomorrow — I'm very nervous.

patterns.label: Hardworking or lazy
patterns.note: A common contrast for describing work ethic: 勤力 (kan4 lik6, hardworking) vs 懶 (laan5, lazy). 佢好勤力 (keoi5 hou2 kan4 lik6) = he's very hardworking.

drills.frameJ: keoi5 jat6 jat6 nou5 lik6 zou6 je5, hou2 ▢.
drills.english: He works hard every day — very hardworking.
drills.frameE: He works hard every day — very …

patterns.label: Saying what hurts
patterns.note: To say something hurts, name the part + 痛 (tung3, pain): 頭痛 (tau4 tung3, headache), 肚痛 (tou5 tung3, stomachache). 我 (ngo5, I) + part + 痛 (tung3) = 'my … hurts'.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 ▢, soeng2 fan3 gaau3.
drills.english: I have a headache, I want to sleep.
drills.frameE: I have a …, I want to sleep.

patterns.label: Naming a body part
patterns.note: The basic body parts: 頭 (tau4, head), 眼 (ngaan5, eyes), 手 (sau2, hand), 腳 (goek3, foot). Point and name them to build the core set.

examples.j: ni1 go3 hai6 ngo5 zek3 sau2.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 jung6 ▢ lo2 je5.
drills.english: I use my hand to pick things up.
drills.frameE: I use my … to pick things up.

patterns.label: Telling the doctor you're sick
patterns.note: Describing illness: 病 (beng6, sick), 發燒 (faat3 siu1, fever), 咳 (kat1, cough). String them together for the doctor — 我病咗，發燒 (ngo5 beng6 zo2, faat3 siu1).

examples.j: ngo5 kat1 dak1 hou2 sai1 lei6.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 hou2 jit6, ho2 nang4 ▢.
drills.english: I feel hot — maybe I have a fever.
drills.frameE: I feel hot — maybe I have a …

patterns.label: Where to get help when ill
patterns.structure: heoi3 + ji1 sang1 / ji1 jyun2 / joek6 fong2
patterns.note: Places and people for illness: 醫生 (ji1 sang1, doctor), 醫院 (ji1 jyun2, hospital), 藥房 (joek6 fong2, pharmacy). 去睇醫生 (heoi3 tai2 ji1 sang1) = go see a doctor.

examples.e: I'm going to see a doctor.

drills.frameJ: beng6 dak1 hou2 jim4 zung6, jiu3 heoi3 ▢.

patterns.label: Asking for medicine
patterns.note: 藥 (joek6) is medicine; 藥房 (joek6 fong2) is the pharmacy (literally 'medicine room'). 我要買藥 (ngo5 jiu3 maai5 joek6) = I need to buy medicine.

drills.frameJ: tau4 tung3, heoi3 joek6 fong2 maai5 di1 ▢.
drills.english: Headache — go to the pharmacy for some medicine.
drills.frameE: Headache — go to the pharmacy for some …

patterns.label: Left or right
patterns.note: 左邊 (zo2 bin1, left side) and 右邊 (jau6 bin1, right side). 喺左邊 (hai2 zo2 bin1) = on the left. The everyday pair for giving directions.

examples.e: The supermarket is on the right.

drills.frameJ: ngan4 hong4 hai2 ▢, m4 hai6 jau6 bin1.
drills.english: The bank is on the left, not the right.
drills.frameE: The bank is on the …, not the right.

patterns.label: In front or behind
patterns.note: 前面 (cin4 min6, in front / ahead) and 後面 (hau6 min6, behind). Useful for 'it's just ahead' or 'right behind you'.

drills.frameJ: ce1 zaam6 hai2 ▢, haang4 do1 gei2 bou6 zau6 dou3.
drills.english: The station is ahead — a few more steps and you're there.
drills.frameE: The station is … — a few more steps and you're there.

patterns.label: Go straight or turn
patterns.note: 直行 (zik6 haang4, go straight) and 轉 (zyun3, turn) are the two core movement verbs for directions. 直行轉左 (zik6 haang4 zyun3 zo2) = go straight then turn left.

drills.frameJ: m4 sai2 zyun3, jat1 zik6 ▢ zau6 dak1.
drills.english: No need to turn — just go straight.
drills.frameE: No need to turn — just … and you're fine.

patterns.label: Near or far
patterns.note: 近 (kan5, close) and 遠 (jyun5, far) — the distance pair. 好近 (hou2 kan5) = very close; 好遠 (hou2 jyun5) = very far.

drills.frameJ: haang4 lou6 zau6 dou3, hou2 ▢.
drills.english: You can walk there — it's very close.
drills.frameE: You can walk there — it's very …

patterns.label: Opposite or nearby
patterns.note: 對面 (deoi3 min6, opposite / across from) and 附近 (fu6 gan6, nearby / in the area). 喺對面 (hai2 deoi3 min6) = right across the way.

drills.frameC: 超市就喺▢,過條馬路就到。
drills.frameJ: ciu1 si5 zau6 hai2 ▢, gwo3 tiu4 maa5 lou6 zau6 dou3.
drills.english: The supermarket is right opposite — cross the road and you're there.
drills.frameE: The supermarket is right … — cross the road and you're there.

patterns.label: Asking for a discount
patterns.note: 有冇折 (jau5 mou5 zit3)? — 'any discount?' — is the standard bargaining opener at a market. 折 (zit3) means a price reduction.

examples.j: maai5 loeng5 gin6 jau5 mou5 zit3?

drills.frameJ: lou5 baan2, ▢ ngo5 jiu3 maai5 saam1 gin6.
drills.english: Boss, any discount? I want three.

patterns.label: Buy or sell
patterns.note: A tricky near-pair: 買 (maai5, buy) and 賣 (maai6, sell) — same characters' cousins, different tone. 買 (maai5) is the rising tone, 賣 (maai6) the low falling. 我想買 (ngo5 soeng2 maai5) = I want to buy.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 soeng2 ▢ ni1 gin6 seot1 saam1.
drills.english: I want to buy this shirt.

patterns.label: Trying clothes for fit
patterns.note: For fit: 緊 (gan2, tight) and 鬆 (sung1, loose). 試吓 (si3 haa5) = try on. 太緊 (taai3 gan2) = too tight.

drills.frameJ: ni1 tiu4 fu3 taai3 ▢, zoek3 m4 lok6.
drills.english: These trousers are too tight — can't get them on.
drills.frameE: These trousers are too … — can't get them on.

patterns.label: Asking for a size
patterns.structure: jau5 mou5 + daai6 maa5 / sai3 maa5?
patterns.note: 尺碼 (cek3 maa5) = size. 大碼 (daai6 maa5, large) and 細碼 (sai3 maa5, small). 有冇大碼 (jau5 mou5 daai6 maa5)? = got a large?

drills.frameJ: ni1 gin6 taai3 sai3, jau5 mou5 ▢?
drills.english: This one's too small — got a large?
drills.frameE: This one's too small — got a …?

patterns.label: Which transport to take
patterns.note: 搭 (daap3) is the verb for taking public transport: 搭巴士 (daap3 baa1 si2, take the bus), 搭的士 (daap3 dik1 si2, take a taxi).

drills.frameJ: sak1 ce1, ngo5 dei6 daap3 ▢ laa1.
drills.english: Traffic jam — let's take the bus.

patterns.label: Telling the taxi where to go
patterns.note: 去邊度 (heoi3 bin1 dou6)? — 'where to?' — is what a taxi driver asks. Answer with your destination.

drills.frameJ: si1 gei1 man6: ▢
drills.english: The driver asks: Where to?

patterns.label: Asking how far
patterns.note: 幾遠 (gei2 jyun5)? — 'how far?'. Pair it with a destination to gauge the trip. 仲有幾遠 (zung6 jau5 gei2 jyun5)? = how much further?

drills.frameJ: si1 gei1, heoi3 gei1 coeng4 ▢
drills.english: Driver, how far is it to the airport?

patterns.label: Telling the driver to stop
patterns.note: 停 (ting4) means 'stop'. On a minibus you call out 有落 or 呢度停 (ni1 dou6 ting4, stop here) to get off.

drills.frameJ: dou3 laa3, ni1 dou6 ▢.
drills.english: We're here — stop here.

patterns.label: My hobby is…
patterns.note: 興趣 (hing3 ceoi3) means hobby / interest. 我嘅興趣係… (ngo5 ge3 hing3 ceoi3 hai6 …) = my hobby is …, then name the activity.

tai2 syu1 hai6 ngo5 hing3 ceoi3.

drills.english: My hobby is hiking — I go every weekend.
drills.frameE: My hobby is … — I go every weekend.

patterns.label: Listening and singing
patterns.structure: ngo5 zung1 ji3 + ting1 go1 / coeng3 go1
patterns.note: Two music hobbies that share 歌 (go1, song): 聽歌 (ting1 go1, listen to music) and 唱歌 (coeng3 go1, sing). 聽 (ting1) = listen, 唱 (coeng3) = sing.

examples.j: keoi5 hou2 zung1 ji3 coeng3 go1.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 heoi3 KTV ▢.
drills.english: I go to KTV to sing.

patterns.label: Creative hobbies
patterns.structure: ngo5 zung1 ji3 + waak6 waa2 / jing2 soeng2
patterns.note: Hands-on hobbies: 畫畫 (waak6 waa2, drawing / painting) and 影相 (jing2 soeng2, taking photos). Both make something to keep.

patterns.structure: ngo5 zung1 ji3 + tiu3 mou5 / haang4 saan1
patterns.note: Get-up-and-move hobbies: 跳舞 (tiu3 mou5, dance) and 行山 (haang4 saan1, hiking). 跳 (tiu3) = jump, 行 (haang4) = walk.

patterns.label: Asking for the menu
patterns.note: 餐牌 (caan1 paai4) is the menu. 唔該餐牌 (m4 goi1 caan1 paai4) = menu, please. 侍應 (si6 jing3) is the waiter who brings it.

drills.english: Waiter, please give us a menu.

patterns.label: Placing your order
patterns.note: 落單 (lok6 daan1) = to place an order; 埋單 (maai4 daan1) = ask for the bill. They bookend the meal — order at the start, settle up at the end.

patterns.label: Asking for the bill
patterns.note: 埋單 (maai4 daan1) is how you ask for the bill — literally 'close the tab'. 唔該埋單 (m4 goi1 maai4 daan1) is the all-purpose phrase at the end of a meal.

drills.frameJ: sik6 baau2 laa3, m4 goi1 ▢.
drills.english: We're full — bill, please.

patterns.label: Saying the food is good
patterns.note: 好食 (hou2 sik6) = delicious (literally 'good to eat'). The natural compliment after a meal: 啲嘢好食 (di1 je5 hou2 sik6) = the food is great.

patterns.note: 銀行 (ngan4 hong4) is the bank; 提款機 (tai4 fun2 gei1) is the ATM. 去銀行 (heoi3 ngan4 hong4) = go to the bank.

patterns.note: 找錢 (zaau2 cin2) is the change you get back; 散紙 (saan3 zi2) is coins / small notes. 唔使找 (m4 sai2 zaau2) = keep the change.

patterns.label: Moving money around
patterns.note: 匯錢 (wui6 cin2) is to transfer money; 唱錢 (coeng3 cin2) is to change currency. Two different 'money moves' — one between accounts, one between currencies.

drills.frameJ: heoi3 leoi5 hang4 zi1 cin4, jiu3 ▢ zou6 gong2 bai6.

patterns.label: Opening an account
patterns.note: 戶口 (wu6 hau2) is a bank account. 開戶口 (hoi1 wu6 hau2) = open an account. 錢 (cin2) is the all-purpose word for money.

examples.e: How much is in the account?

patterns.label: People at school
patterns.structure: lou5 si1 / hok6 saang1 / tung4 hok6
patterns.note: The cast at school: 老師 (lou5 si1, teacher), 學生 (hok6 saang1, student), 同學 (tung4 hok6, classmate). 我係學生 (ngo5 hai6 hok6 saang1) = I'm a student.

patterns.label: Doing schoolwork
patterns.note: 功課 (gung1 fo3) is homework; 讀書 (duk6 syu1) is to study. 做功課 (zou6 gung1 fo3) = do homework.

patterns.label: Going to class
patterns.note: 上堂 (soeng5 tong4) is to attend class; 考試 (haau2 si3) is an exam. 上堂 (soeng5 tong4) literally 'go up to the hall'.

patterns.label: Knowing how / answering
patterns.note: 識 (sik1) means 'know how to'; 答 (daap3) means 'answer'. 我識答 (ngo5 sik1 daap3) = I know how to answer it.

drills.frameJ: lou5 si1 man6 man6 tai4, ngo5 geoi2 sau2 ▢.

patterns.label: Talking about your school
patterns.note: 學校 (hok6 haau6) is school. Notice 學 (hok6, learn) appears in 學校 (hok6 haau6, school), 學生 (hok6 saang1, student) and 同學 (tung4 hok6, classmate) — the shared root for 'learning'.

examples.j: ngo5 ge3 hok6 haau6 hou2 daai6.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 mui5 jat6 faan1 ▢ duk6 syu1.

patterns.label: Start and finish work
patterns.note: 返工 (faan1 gung1) is to start/go to work; 放工 (fong3 gung1) is to finish work. The bookends of the working day.

patterns.label: People at the office
patterns.note: 老闆 (lou5 baan2) is the boss; 同事 (tung4 si6) is a colleague. Note 同事 (tung4 si6, colleague) mirrors 同學 (tung4 hok6, classmate) — 同 (tung4) means 'same / fellow'.

patterns.label: Meetings and overtime
patterns.note: 開會 (hoi1 wui2) is to have a meeting; 加班 (gaa1 baan1) is to work overtime. The two things that eat up the workday.

drills.frameJ: zou6 m4 saai3 di1 je5, gam1 maan5 jiu3 ▢.

patterns.label: Payday and deadlines

patterns.note: 出糧 (ceot1 loeng4) is payday — 'the salary comes out'; 截止日期 (zit6 zi2 jat6 kei4) is the deadline. The carrot and the stick of work.

drills.english: I work at a big company.

patterns.label: Devices
patterns.note: 電腦 (din6 nou5) is a computer — literally 'electric brain'; 電話 (din6 waa2) is a phone — 'electric speech'. Both share 電 (din6, electric).

patterns.label: Getting online
patterns.note: 上網 (soeng5 mong5) is to go online — 'get on the net'. You'll need 訊號 (seon3 hou6, signal) or WiFi to do it.

patterns.label: Logging in
patterns.note: 密碼 (mat6 maa5) is the password; many apps need one to get in. 程式 (cing4 sik1) is an app or program.

WiFi mat6 maa5 hai6 mat1 je5?

patterns.label: Battery and signal
patterns.note: 充電 (cung1 din6) is to charge the battery; 訊號 (seon3 hou6) is the phone signal. The two things you check when your phone struggles.

drills.frameJ: dak1 faan1 siu2 siu2 din6, jiu3 faai3 di1 ▢.
drills.english: Battery's low — need to charge it soon.

patterns.label: When it's broken
patterns.note: 壞 (waai6) means broken / not working; 屏幕 (ping4 mok6) is the screen. 壞咗 (waai6 zo2) = it's broken (with the completed-action 咗 zo2).

drills.frameJ: bou6 din6 waa2 dit3 zo2 lok6 dei6, ▢ zo2.
drills.english: The phone fell on the floor — it's broken.
drills.frameE: The phone fell on the floor — it's … now.

patterns.label: Hot or cold day
patterns.note: 熱 (jit6, hot) and 凍 (dung3, cold) — the basic temperature pair. 今日好凍 (gam1 jat6 hou2 dung3) = it's cold today.

drills.frameJ: dung1 tin1 lai4 laa3, gam1 jat6 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: Winter's here — it's cold today.

patterns.label: Rain and sun
patterns.note: 落雨 (lok6 jyu5) is raining — 'rain falls'; 太陽 (taai3 joeng4) is the sun. 落雨 (lok6 jyu5) needs an umbrella; 太陽 (taai3 joeng4) needs sunscreen.

examples.e: Bring an umbrella when it rains.

drills.frameJ: gei3 dak1 daai3 ze1, ceot1 min6 ▢.
drills.english: Remember an umbrella — it's raining outside.

patterns.label: Wind and typhoon
patterns.note: 風 (fung1) is wind; 颱風 (toi4 fung1) is a typhoon — a defining feature of Hong Kong summers. 颱風 contains 風 (fung1).

examples.j: toi4 fung1 m4 sai2 faan1 gung1.

drills.frameC: 天文台話有▢,要留喺屋企。
drills.frameJ: tin1 man4 toi4 waa6 jau5 ▢, jiu3 lau4 hai2 uk1 kei2.
drills.english: The observatory says there's a typhoon — stay home.
drills.frameE: The observatory says there's a … — stay home.

patterns.label: Humid or cloudy
patterns.note: 潮濕 (ciu4 sap1) is humid — Hong Kong's spring weather; 雲 (wan4) is cloud. 好潮濕 (hou2 ciu4 sap1) = very humid / muggy.

drills.frameJ: faan1 ciu4 laa3, gaan1 uk1 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: It's the wet season — the flat is very humid.
drills.frameE: It's the wet season — the flat is very …

patterns.label: Checking in and out
patterns.note: 入住 (jap6 zyu6) is to check in; 退房 (teoi3 fong2) is to check out. 訂房 (deng6 fong2) is to book a room beforehand.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 dou3 zau2 dim3 laa3, soeng2 ▢.
drills.english: I've arrived at the hotel — I'd like to check in.
drills.frameE: I've arrived at the hotel — I'd like to …

patterns.label: Your room and key
patterns.note: 房間 (fong4 gaan1) is the room; 鎖匙 (so2 si4) is the key. 幾樓 (gei2 lau2) asks what floor.

examples.j: ngo5 ge3 fong4 gaan1 hai2 saam1 lau2.
examples.e: My room is on the third floor.

patterns.label: Luggage and breakfast
patterns.note: 行李 (hang4 lei5) is luggage; 早餐 (zou2 caan1) is breakfast — often included at hotels. 服務員 (fuk6 mou6 jyun4) is the staff who help with both.

drills.frameC: 服務員,唔該幫我攞▢上房。
drills.frameJ: fuk6 mou6 jyun4, m4 goi1 bong1 ngo5 lo2 ▢ soeng5 fong2.
drills.english: Staff, please help carry my luggage up to the room.
drills.frameE: Staff, please help carry my … up to the room.

patterns.label: Asking the staff
patterns.note: 服務員 (fuk6 mou6 jyun4) is the service staff; 幾樓 (gei2 lau2) asks 'what floor'. 樓 (lau2) means floor / storey.

examples.j: fuk6 mou6 jyun4, zou2 caan1 hai2 gei2 lau2?
examples.e: Staff, what floor is breakfast on?

examples.j: gin6 san1 sat1 hai2 gei2 lau2?
examples.e: What floor is the gym on?

drills.english: I ask the staff: what floor is breakfast on?
drills.frameE: I ask the staff: breakfast is on … floor?

patterns.label: Cats and other pets
patterns.note: 寵物 (cung2 mat6) is a pet; 養 (joeng5) is to keep/raise one. Common pets: 貓 (maau1, cat), 鳥 (niu5, bird), 兔仔 (tou3 zai2, rabbit).

examples.j: ngo5 joeng5 zo2 jat1 zek3 maau1.

drills.frameC: 我屋企養咗一隻▢,成日捉老鼠。
drills.frameJ: ngo5 uk1 kei2 joeng5 zo2 jat1 zek3 ▢, sing4 jat6 zuk1 lou5 syu2.
drills.english: I keep a cat at home — it always catches mice.
drills.frameE: I keep a … at home — it always catches mice.

patterns.label: Farm animals
patterns.note: Farm animals: 馬 (maa5, horse), 牛 (ngau4, cow), 豬 (zyu1, pig). 牛 (ngau4) also gives 牛肉 (ngau4 juk6, beef) and 豬 (zyu1) gives 豬肉 (zyu1 juk6, pork).

examples.j: nung4 coeng4 jau5 maa5 tung4 ngau4.
examples.e: The farm has horses and cows.

drills.frameC: 農場有一隻▢,可以畀人騎。
drills.frameJ: nung4 coeng4 jau5 jat1 zek3 ▢, ho2 ji5 bei2 jan4 ke4.
drills.english: The farm has a horse you can ride.
drills.frameE: The farm has a … you can ride.

patterns.label: Keeping a pet
patterns.note: 養 (joeng5) means to keep or raise an animal; 寵物 (cung2 mat6) is a pet. 養寵物 (joeng5 cung2 mat6) = keep a pet.

examples.e: I want to keep a pet.

examples.j: joeng5 gau2 jiu3 hou2 jau5 noi6 sing3.
nei5 joeng5 mat1 je5 cung2 mat6?

drills.frameJ: sai3 lou6 soeng2 ▢ jat1 zek3 siu2 dung6 mat6.
drills.english: The child wants to keep a small animal.
drills.frameE: The child wants to … a small animal.

patterns.label: That's so cute
patterns.note: 可愛 (ho2 oi3) means cute / adorable — the natural reaction to a 寵物 (cung2 mat6, pet). 好可愛 (hou2 ho2 oi3) = so cute.

drills.frameJ: zek3 tou3 zai2 mou4 jung4 jung4, zan1 hai6 hou2 ▢.
drills.english: The rabbit is fluffy — really so cute.
drills.frameE: The rabbit is fluffy — really so …

patterns.label: Buying a ticket
patterns.note: 門票 (mun4 piu3) is the entry ticket; 入場 (jap6 coeng4) is entry/admission. 買門票 (maai5 mun4 piu3) = buy a ticket.

drills.frameJ: jap6 heoi3 zi1 cin4 jiu3 maai5 ▢.
drills.english: Before going in you need to buy a ticket.

patterns.label: Asking opening hours
patterns.note: 開幾點 (hoi1 gei2 dim2)? asks 'what time does it open?'. 開放 (hoi1 fong3) means open to visitors. Both share 開 (hoi1, open).

drills.english: Want to go to the museum — first ask what time it opens.

patterns.label: Queue and entry
patterns.note: 排隊 (paai4 deoi2) is to queue / line up; 入場 (jap6 coeng4) is entry. At a busy attraction you 排隊 (paai4 deoi2) before 入場 (jap6 coeng4).

drills.frameJ: jan4 hou2 do1, ngo5 dei6 jiu3 ▢ sin1 jap6 dou2 coeng4.
drills.english: Lots of people — we have to queue before we can get in.

patterns.label: Photos and souvenirs
patterns.structure: paak3 ziu3 / maai5 gei2 nim6 ban2
patterns.note: 拍照 (paak3 ziu3) is to take photos (at a sight); 紀念品 (gei2 nim6 ban2) is a souvenir. The two things tourists collect.

examples.j: ho2 m4 ho2 ji5 paak3 ziu3?

drills.frameJ: fung1 ging2 gam3 leng3, gang2 hai6 jiu3 ▢.
drills.english: The view is so beautiful — of course I'll take photos.
drills.frameE: The view is so beautiful — of course I'll …

patterns.label: Map or guide
patterns.note: 地圖 (dei6 tou4) is a map; 導遊 (dou6 jau4) is a tour guide. 景點 (ging2 dim2) is the attraction itself.

examples.j: ni1 go3 ging2 dim2 hou2 ceot1 meng2.

drills.frameJ: m4 sik1 lou6, ho2 ji5 tai2 haa5 ▢.
drills.english: Don't know the way — can look at the map.
drills.frameE: Don't know the way — can look at the …

patterns.label: Cooking methods
patterns.note: Three core methods: 煮 (zyu2, cook/boil), 炒 (caau2, stir-fry), 蒸 (zing1, steam). 炒菜 (caau2 coi3) = stir-fry vegetables.

drills.frameC: 廣東人鍾意▢魚,保持鮮味。
drills.frameJ: gwong2 dung1 jan4 zung1 ji3 ▢ jyu2, bou2 ci4 sin1 mei6.
drills.english: Cantonese people like to steam fish to keep it fresh.
drills.frameE: Cantonese people like to … fish to keep it fresh.

patterns.label: Seasoning
patterns.note: 鹽 (jim4) is salt; 糖 (tong4) is sugar. 加鹽 (gaa1 jim4) = add salt. The two basic seasonings to balance a dish.

drills.frameJ: go3 tong1 taam5 zo2, gaa1 do1 siu2 siu2 ▢.
drills.english: The soup is bland — add a bit more salt.
drills.frameE: The soup is bland — add a bit more …

patterns.label: Oil and sauce
patterns.note: 油 (jau4) is oil; 醬油 (zoeng3 jau4) is soy sauce — note 醬油 contains 油 (jau4). Both go in the 鑊 (wok6, wok).

drills.frameJ: caau2 zi1 cin4, sin1 hai2 wok6 dou6 lok6 di1 ▢.
drills.english: Before stir-frying, put some oil in the wok first.
drills.frameE: Before stir-frying, put some … in the wok first.

patterns.label: Prep work
patterns.note: 切 (cit3) is to cut; 食材 (sik6 coi4) are the ingredients. 切食材 (cit3 sik6 coi4) = cut the ingredients — the prep before cooking.

drills.frameJ: zyu2 faan6 zi1 cin4, jiu3 ▢ hou2 di1 so1 coi3.
drills.english: Before cooking, cut the vegetables.

patterns.label: Using the wok
patterns.note: 鑊 (wok6) is the wok — the heart of a Cantonese kitchen. 食材 (sik6 coi4, ingredients) go into the 鑊 to be 炒 (caau2, stir-fried).

drills.frameC: 炒菜要用個大▢,夠熱先好食。
drills.frameJ: caau2 coi3 jiu3 jung6 go3 daai6 ▢, gau3 jit6 sin1 hou2 sik6.
drills.english: Stir-frying needs a big wok — hot enough to taste good.
drills.frameE: Stir-frying needs a big … — hot enough to taste good.

patterns.label: Calling for help
patterns.note: 救命 (gau3 meng6)! literally 'save (my) life' — the cry for help in danger. 救 (gau3) means save/rescue, also in 救護車 (gau3 wu6 ce1, ambulance).

drills.frameJ: dit3 zo2 lok6 seoi2, daai6 aai3 ▢!
drills.english: Fell in the water — shout for help!

patterns.label: Calling the police
patterns.note: 報警 (bou3 ging2) is to call the police; 警察 (ging2 caat3) are the police themselves. Both share 警 (ging2). The HK emergency number is 999 (gau2 gau2 gau2).

drills.frameJ: uk1 kei2 bei2 jan4 baau3 sit3, zik1 hak1 ▢.
drills.english: The house was burgled — call the police right away.
drills.frameE: The house was burgled — … right away.

patterns.label: Fire and danger
patterns.note: 火 (fo2) is fire; 危險 (ngai4 him2) means dangerous. 火 (fo2) also appears in 火車 (fo2 ce1, train) — but here it's the emergency.

examples.e: There's a fire — get out quick.

drills.frameJ: cyu4 fong2 zoek6 ▢ laa3, hou2 ngai4 him2!
drills.english: The kitchen's caught fire — very dangerous!

patterns.label: Getting medical help
patterns.structure: giu3 + gau3 wu6 ce1 / heoi3 gap1 zing3 sat1
patterns.note: 救護車 (gau3 wu6 ce1) is an ambulance; 急症室 (gap1 zing3 sat1) is A&E / the ER. 受傷 (sau6 soeng1) means injured — when you need them.

drills.frameJ: keoi5 sau6 zo2 soeng1, faai3 di1 giu3 ▢.
drills.english: He's injured — call an ambulance quick.

patterns.label: Get away
patterns.note: 走 (zau2) means flee / escape (also 'leave' in everyday use). 受傷 (sau6 soeng1) is to be injured — what you avoid by 走 (zau2)-ing from danger.

drills.frameJ: jau5 fo2 zuk1, daai6 gaa1 faai3 di1 ▢!
drills.english: There's a fire — everyone get out quick!

patterns.label: Making plans
patterns.note: 朋友 (pang4 jau5) is a friend; 約 (joek3) is to make plans / arrange to meet. 約朋友 (joek3 pang4 jau5) = make plans with a friend.

examples.e: Make plans to eat with a friend.

drills.frameC: 週末得閒,我想▢幾個朋友出嚟。
drills.frameJ: zau1 mut6 dak1 haan4, ngo5 soeng2 ▢ gei2 go3 pang4 jau5 ceot1 lai4.
drills.english: Free at the weekend — I want to make plans with a few friends.
drills.frameE: Free at the weekend — I want to … a few friends out.

patterns.label: Are you free?
patterns.note: 得閒 (dak1 haan4) means free / having spare time. 你得唔得閒 (nei5 dak1 m4 dak1 haan4)? = are you free? The opener before making plans.

examples.j: dak1 haan4 jat1 cai4 sik6 faan6.

drills.frameJ: ting1 jat6 nei5 ▢ maa3? jat1 cai4 heoi3 tai2 hei3.
drills.english: Are you free tomorrow? Let's go see a movie.
drills.frameE: Tomorrow are you …? Let's go see a movie.

patterns.label: Going out together
patterns.note: 一齊 (jat1 cai4) means together; 出街 (ceot1 gaai1) is to go out (literally 'out to the street'). 一齊出街 (jat1 cai4 ceot1 gaai1) = go out together.

drills.frameC: 唔好留喺屋企,我哋▢出街啦。
drills.frameJ: m4 hou2 lau4 hai2 uk1 kei2, ngo5 dei6 ▢ ceot1 gaai1 laa1.
drills.english: Don't stay home — let's go out together.
drills.frameE: Don't stay home — let's go out … .

patterns.label: Inviting to a party
patterns.note: 邀請 (jiu1 cing2) is to invite (more formal than 約); 派對 (paai3 deoi3) is a party — a loan from English 'party'. 慶祝 (hing3 zuk1) = celebrate.

examples.j: jiu1 cing2 nei5 lai4 paai3 deoi3.

drills.frameC: 我生日,想▢你哋嚟我屋企。
drills.frameJ: ngo5 saang1 jat6, soeng2 ▢ nei5 dei6 lai4 ngo5 uk1 kei2.
drills.english: It's my birthday — I want to invite you all to my place.
drills.frameE: It's my birthday — I want to … you all to my place.

patterns.label: Rain check
patterns.note: 改日 (goi2 jat6) means 'another day' — a polite rain check when you can't make it. 改 (goi2) = change, 日 (jat6) = day.

examples.j: gam1 jat6 m4 dak1, goi2 jat6 laa1.

drills.frameJ: gam1 jat6 m4 dak1 haan4, bat1 jyu4 ▢ sin1 laa1.
drills.english: Not free today — let's do it another day.
drills.frameE: Not free today — let's do it … instead.

patterns.label: Rooms of the home
patterns.structure: cyu4 fong2 / haak3 teng1 / ci3 so2
patterns.note: 屋企 (uk1 kei2) is home. Inside: 廚房 (cyu4 fong2, kitchen), 客廳 (haak3 teng1, living room), 廁所 (ci3 so2, toilet).

examples.e: Watch TV in the living room.

drills.frameJ: tou5 o1, soeng2 heoi3 ▢.
drills.english: Upset stomach — need the toilet.

patterns.label: Furniture
patterns.note: 床 (cong4) is a bed, 枱 (toi2) a table, 椅 (ji2) a chair — the basics in a 房 (fong2, room).

drills.frameJ: fan3 gaau3 ge3 si4 hau6, fan3 hai2 zoeng1 ▢ dou6.
drills.english: When sleeping, you sleep on the bed.
drills.frameE: When sleeping, you sleep on the …

patterns.label: Doors and windows
patterns.note: 門 (mun4) is a door; 窗 (coeng1) is a window. 開門 (hoi1 mun4) = open the door; 開窗 (hoi1 coeng1) = open the window.

drills.frameJ: gaan1 fong2 hou2 guk6, hoi1 go3 ▢ tau3 haa5 hei3.
drills.english: The room is stuffy — open the window for some air.
drills.frameE: The room is stuffy — open the … for some air.

patterns.label: Talking about your home
patterns.note: 屋企 (uk1 kei2) means home / one's place. 我屋企 (ngo5 uk1 kei2) = my home — no possessive particle needed, like family words.

drills.frameJ: je6 laa3, ngo5 jiu3 faan1 ▢ fan3 gaau3.
drills.english: It's late — I need to go home to sleep.
drills.frameE: It's late — I need to go … to sleep.

patterns.label: The kitchen and living room
patterns.note: 廚房 (cyu4 fong2) is where you cook; 客廳 (haak3 teng1) is where guests sit — 客 (haak3) means guest. The two main shared rooms.

examples.e: The kitchen has lots of stuff.
The living room has a sofa.

drills.frameJ: zyu2 faan6 zing2 je5 sik6, gang2 hai6 hai2 ▢.
drills.english: Cooking food, of course, happens in the kitchen.
drills.frameE: Cooking food, of course, happens in the …

patterns.label: Doing exercise
patterns.note: 運動 (wan6 dung6) is sport / exercise (the general word); 健身 (gin6 san1) is working out / the gym. 做運動 (zou6 wan6 dung6) = do exercise.

examples.j: zou6 wan6 dung6 hou2 gin6 hong1.

drills.frameJ: soeng2 san1 tai2 hou2, jiu3 do1 di1 zou6 ▢.
drills.english: To be healthy, do more exercise.

patterns.label: Running and swimming
patterns.note: 跑步 (paau2 bou6) is running / jogging; 游水 (jau4 seoi2) is swimming. Two solo activities — 跑 (paau2) = run, 游 (jau4) = swim.

drills.frameJ: tin1 hei3 jit6, ngo5 zung1 ji3 heoi3 ▢ siu1 syu2.
drills.english: Hot weather — I like to swim to cool off.
drills.frameE: Hot weather — I like to … to cool off.

patterns.label: Ball games
patterns.structure: daa2 bo1 / zuk1 kau4 / laam4 kau4
patterns.note: 打波 (daa2 bo1) is to play ball games generally; specific ones: 足球 (zuk1 kau4, football), 籃球 (laam4 kau4, basketball). 波 (bo1) is a colloquial word for ball.

examples.j: ngo5 zung1 ji3 tek3 zuk1 kau4.

drills.frameJ: ngo5 dei6 jat1 deoi6 sap6 jat1 go3 jan4, tek3 ▢.
drills.english: Our team has eleven players — we play football.
drills.frameE: Our team has eleven players — we play …

patterns.label: On the court
patterns.note: 球場 (kau4 coeng4) is the court / field; 隊 (deoi6) is a team. 場 (coeng4) means a ground/venue — same character as in 商場 (soeng1 coeng4, mall).

examples.e: Go to the court to play.

drills.frameJ: gau3 jan4 laa3, heoi3 ▢ tek3 bo1 laa1.
drills.english: We have enough people — let's go to the field to play.
drills.frameE: We have enough people — let's go to the … to play.

patterns.label: Winning the game
patterns.note: 贏 (jeng4) is to win; 隊 (deoi6) is the team. 我哋贏咗 (ngo5 dei6 jeng4 zo2) = we won. The opposite is 輸 (syu1, lose).

drills.frameC: 最後一分鐘入波,我哋▢咗！
drills.frameJ: zeoi3 hau6 jat1 fan1 zung1 jap6 bo1, ngo5 dei6 ▢ zo2!
